h1: Why blended Scotch deserves another look
title: Why Blended Scotch Deserves Another Look | Craft Beer School
desc: Why blended Scotch is worth tasting seriously: how malt and grain whisky are combined, what the blender does and how to taste a blend properly.
teaser: Single malt gets the attention. Most Scotch sold is blended. The best blends are hard work to make.
standfirst: Many whisky fans move from blends to single malts and never look back. That is a pity. Blended Scotch is the backbone of the category. A good blend is one of the hardest things in whisky to make well.
sections:
A blended Scotch combines malt whisky and grain whisky. Malt whisky is made from malted barley in pot stills. Grain whisky is made mostly from other cereals such as wheat or maize, with some malted barley, in column stills. Both must mature at least three years in oak casks in Scotland.

A blend can include whisky from dozens of distilleries. Blended malt is a separate category: only malt whiskies from several distilleries, no grain. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky lays out every category.

Blends make up the large majority of Scotch sold around the world. The single malt boom is recent by comparison.

Grain whisky is often dismissed as filler. It is better understood as structure. It is lighter in body and flavour than malt, with a clean sweetness, cereal and soft vanilla from the cask. In a blend it carries the malt whiskies, rounds off their edges and gives the whole a smooth, drinkable texture.

It also makes blends affordable. Column stills run continuously and produce spirit far more efficiently than pot stills. The Coffey still, patented by Aeneas Coffey in 1830, made blended Scotch possible on a large scale.

A master blender's job is consistency. Every bottle of a brand should taste the same, year after year, even though no two casks are identical and distilleries change. The blender noses samples from hundreds of casks, often diluted to around 20% ABV so the alcohol does not numb the nose. Then they build a recipe that hits the house style.

When one whisky runs short, the blender has to find another that fills the same role. That takes a deep memory for aroma and a precise vocabulary. Our guide to how blenders keep brands consistent describes the process.

In other words, a blend is not a lesser single malt. It is a different achievement.
How to taste a blend fairly

Most people drink blends with soda, water or ice. That is fine. Many blends are designed for it. To judge one properly, though, taste it neat first.

  • Pour 15 ml into a tulip glass, the same as you would for a single malt.
  • Nose for the grain: light sweetness, vanilla, cereal.
  • Look for the malt underneath: fruit, honey, sometimes a wisp of smoke.
  • Taste, then add a few drops of water and taste again.

Ask yourself whether the parts feel joined or whether you can taste the seams. A good blend feels like one whisky.

Blended Scotch sits on many Indian shelves alongside Indian whiskies, which are often blends of a different kind, made with some malt or grain whisky together with neutral spirit. Comparing a blended Scotch with an Indian blend at a similar price is an instructive tasting. It shows the difference that matured grain whisky makes in place of unaged neutral spirit.

Blends also suit how India drinks. A highball with plenty of ice in a hot summer, or a whisky with water at dinner, is exactly what many blends were built for. Count each measure all the same and keep water on the table.

An age statement on a blend works the same way as on a single malt: it gives the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle, grain included. A 12 year old blend contains no malt or grain younger than 12 years. Many everyday blends carry no age at all, which means only that every component meets the three year minimum.

The words matter too. Blended Scotch whisky means malt plus grain. Blended malt Scotch whisky means malts only. Single grain Scotch whisky is grain whisky from one distillery, bottled without malt. Strength usually sits at 40%, the legal floor, because blends are often made for mixing. A blend bottled at 43% or more, or one that states natural colour, is usually aimed at people who will drink it neat.
Premium blends are worth seeking out

Above the everyday blends sit older and premium blends, often with higher malt content and age statements. Some include very old grain whisky, which develops rich toffee, tropical fruit and coconut notes after decades in oak.

These bottles reward the same attention you would give a single malt. Tasting one blind alongside a single malt at a similar price is a humbling exercise for anyone who has written blends off. Picking out the parts, the grain, the fruity malts and the cask influence, is a skill. It is learnt by tasting with intent, not by reading labels.

Buy a blended Scotch you would normally use for highballs and taste 15 ml neat in a proper glass. Write down what you find from the grain and what from the malt. Then make a highball with it and see what survives the soda. You will never taste a blend carelessly again.
faqs: A blend of malt whisky and grain whisky, often from many distilleries, all matured at least three years in oak in Scotland.
Is blended Scotch worse than single malt?
No. Blending is a different skill, aimed at balance and consistency. Some blends beat single malts at the same price.
What is the difference between blended Scotch and blended malt?
Blended Scotch contains malt and grain whisky. Blended malt contains only malt whiskies from more than one distillery.
